opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it changed it quite a lot, though maybe not in the way people expect.

Before Stanford, I thought of starting a company as something very far away, something you do after you've finished the "real" work. In research you're trained to think in terms of papers and ideas, and entrepreneurship felt like a different world with different rules. At Stanford that boundary just feels much thinner. You're surrounded by people who move back and forth all the time: a PhD student this year, a founder next year, then back to a lab or a big company. Nobody treats it as a dramatic, irreversible decision. It's just another way to push an idea into the world.

The biggest shift for me was psychological. I used to think you needed a fully formed plan, a perfect product, a clear market, before you were "allowed" to start. At Stanford I saw that many people start with a strong conviction about a technical direction and a willingness to iterate, and they figure out the rest along the way. Failure is also much less stigmatized. If you try something and it doesn't work, people see it as experience rather than a mark against you.

At the same time, being there made me more careful in one respect. When you see so many startups up close, you realize that a good idea in a paper is not the same as a good company. You need timing, a team, a real user need, and a lot of stamina. So I'd say Stanford made me more open to the idea of starting something, but also more honest with myself about why I'd want to do it, and whether the problem actually needs a company rather than just a good paper or an open-source project.

r001.rationale: He says Stanford surrounded him with people moving into and out of startups, which made starting a company feel like a more ordinary, accessible option.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, before Stanford, starting a company felt like something other people did. I came from a very academic track, and the default path in my head was: do a PhD, publish papers, maybe become a professor. Entrepreneurship seemed risky and a little bit distant from the kind of work I cared about.

What changed at Stanford was mostly the environment. It wasn't that someone sat me down and told me to found a company. It was that everyone around me treated it as a completely normal option. Your labmate would casually mention they were raising a round. Your classmate from a seminar would drop out for a semester to build something and then come back. Professors themselves had companies on the side. So the psychological barrier just dissolved. It went from "this is a big, scary leap" to "this is one of several reasonable things a person like me can do."

The second thing was seeing how close research and real products actually are, especially in AI right now. In a lot of fields there's a long gap between a paper and anything useful. But at Stanford I watched ideas go from a lab discussion to a demo to a company in a matter of months. That made me realize that if you have a genuinely good idea, a company can sometimes be the fastest way to find out whether it's true, because the market gives you feedback much faster than reviewers do.

And the third thing, which I think is underrated, is that failure is treated differently there. If a startup doesn't work out, nobody thinks less of you. People talk about their failed companies the way they'd talk about a research project that didn't pan out. Once you internalize that, the downside risk feels much smaller, and your calculation about whether to try changes a lot.

So I wouldn't say Stanford made me want to start a company for its own sake. It made me stop seeing it as a separate world, and start seeing it as a tool I could pick up when the right problem showed up.

r001.rationale: He says Stanford’s environment made entrepreneurship feel like a normal option, citing labmates raising money, classmates building companies, and professors with companies.

astra-6.text: Being at Stanford made starting a company feel much more tangible. When you’re surrounded by people who are thinking about building something, you start to see entrepreneurship as a path you could take yourself. For me, the shift was from asking, “Could I ever start a company?” to asking, “What would be worth building?”

r001.rationale: The candidate says the shift came from being surrounded by people thinking about building something, which made entrepreneurship feel like a path they could take.

sol-6.1.text: I think it made starting a company feel like a real option. When you’re surrounded by people who are thinking about building things, you start asking, “Could I do that too?” But there’s a difference between being excited about entrepreneurship and having a problem you really want to solve. For me, the useful shift was to think less about becoming a founder and more about whether something I was working on could actually be useful to people.
